articles.title: How the US power rivalry with Russia and China is turning outer space into the next battlefront
paragraphs: U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink recently confirmed that the United States has weapons deployed in Earth’s orbit . To date, the U.S. Space Force, the space service branch of the U.S. armed forces, has provided relatively few details about what these weapons are or what they can do except that they are what Meink called “on-orbit space control weapons.”

Meink’s announcement is significant, but not necessarily because the U.S. is the first country to place weapons in orbit. For years, the U.S., Russia and China have accused each other of developing and testing such capabilities, although none has publicly acknowledged deploying space weapons – until now.

We are scholars of space law and governance, and our research illustrates the challenges of uniting diverse groups to establish norms related to the use of resources, safety zones and conflict prevention in new domains such as space. Without better communication and deeper coordination between the world’s space powers, we could witness the beginning of a space arms race.
In 1981, the United Nations added the Prevention of an Arms Race in Outer Space, known as PAROS, to its agenda.
More than four decades of diplomatic efforts under PAROS have produced meager results, though there was a United Nations agreement in 2024 that made progress on reducing threats.

Despite many countries’ proclamations supporting space arms control, no multilateral treaty banning weapons in space has been adopted. With global arms control generally in retreat, and the apparent lack of political will among the three major space powers, efforts to control space weapons have reached an impasse.
The question increasingly is not whether an arms race in space can be prevented, but how it will be managed.
The Outer Space Treaty of 1967, to which all major space powers are parties, is often described by scholars, practitioners and policymakers as the constitution of outer space.

Article IV of the treaty remains the only legally binding international provision specifically regulating weapons in outer space. The article prohibits countries from placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit around Earth. It also imposes a broader prohibition on military activities on the Moon and other celestial bodies, including establishing military bases, testing weapons and conducting military maneuvers.

However, the article does not prohibit conventional weapons in Earth’s orbit. That omission is significant. The treaty can be understood as implicitly permitting what it does not prohibit : the placement of such weapons in orbit.

China has used these ambiguities as cover for its own space weaponization efforts. In a 2007 test, China destroyed one of its own satellites while in orbit, and it has recently deployed a mysterious space plane .

China, nonetheless, reacted critically to the recent U.S. weapons announcement. In September 2026, it urged Washington to stop expanding its military presence in space . That same month, Russia renewed calls for the demilitarization of outer space .

Both countries have long advocated stronger international restrictions on space weapons. Russia and China twice jointly proposed a treaty prohibiting the placement of weapons in outer space . The U.S. opposed the proposals in 2014, pointing to their failure to also cover important ground-based, anti-satellite weapons.
But Russian and Chinese declarations in favor of keeping weapons out of space sit uneasily alongside their own activities.

In 2020, U.S. Space Command, part of the Defense Department, accused Russia of testing a space-based anti-satellite weapon after an orbiting Russian satellite released a projectile. Russia said the spacecraft was performing an inspection mission.
In 2024, the United States said Russia had launched another satellite, Cosmos 2576, which it assessed to be a “counter space” weapon capable of attacking other satellites .

China has similarly demonstrated increasingly sophisticated operations in orbit. Five Chinese spacecraft conducted satellite flybys in 2024, an exercise that a senior U.S. Space Force officer later described as practicing “dogfighting in space.”

None of this proves that every suspicious Russian or Chinese spacecraft is a weapon. Many technologies used for servicing, inspection and maneuvering around satellites are inherently dual-use. But it does put Moscow’s and Beijing’s calls to keep weapons out of space in perspective.

It also illustrates the security threat now taking shape. Washington can point to Russian and Chinese activities to justify its own weapons. Moscow and Beijing can now point to acknowledged U.S. weapons to help justify their actions, which could result in a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Space has been part of warfare for decades. The 1991 Gulf War has sometimes been called the first “space war” because of the unprecedented role satellites played in navigation, communications, intelligence and targeting. But satellites primarily supported military operations taking place on the ground.
That distinction has gradually eroded. NATO formally recognized space as a military theater in 2019 .
Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine then demonstrated something different, in which the very definition of a weapon was challenged.

Hours before Russian troops crossed the border, a cyberattack disrupted the U.S. satellite network Viasat, in what was dubbed by commentators as the first “ space-cyber war .” Space-based services were no longer merely supporting military operations but were themselves deliberately targeted as part of a military campaign.

The acknowledgment of weapons in orbit represents another step in that evolution. Space assets are transitioning from systems that primarily support warfare in other domains to systems that can be weapons, targets and participants in combat and are often replete with vulnerabilities that could be exploited by an adversary.

That does not mean future space warfare will resemble Star Wars dogfights or Starfleet armadas taking on Borg cubes. But the emerging battlefield is likely to be much more complicated. Satellites can be disrupted through jamming and spoofing, disabled through cyberattacks, approached or manipulated by other spacecraft, attacked from Earth or potentially attacked by weapons already in orbit.

This makes the connection between space and cyberspace particularly important. A country seeking to neutralize an adversary’s satellites may have several options, ranging from a cyberattack or electronic interference to physically damaging it. At the same time, space-based critical infrastructure has never been more vital to the functioning of the global economy.
Military strategy therefore has to adapt not merely to warfare in space but to warfare across an increasingly interconnected space-cyber nexus .

The important question is no longer whether space will become militarized. It has been militarized for decades. Nor is it even whether states will develop weapons capable of affecting objects in space. Several already have done so.

articles.title: Canadian football
paragraphs: Canadian football, or simply football, is a sport in Canada in which two teams of 12 players compete on a field 110 yards (101 m) long and 65 yards (59 m) wide, attempting to advance a pointed oval-shaped ball into the opposing team's end zone.

Canadian and American football have shared origins and are closely related, but have some significant differences. Canadian football is played with three downs, goalposts in the front of the end zone, and twelve players on each side. American football has four downs, goalposts in the back of the end zone, and eleven players on each side. Canadian football is also played on a wider and longer field, with deeper end zones.

Rugby football, from which Canadian football developed, was first recorded in Canada in the early 1860s, taken there by British immigrants, possibly in 1824. Both the Canadian Football League (CFL), the sport's professional league, and Football Canada, the governing body for amateur play, trace their roots to 1880 and the founding of the Canadian Rugby Football Union. The CFL championship game, the Grey Cup, is one of Canada's biggest sporting events, attracting a large television audience.

Canadian football is also played at high school, junior, collegiate, and semi-professional levels. The Canadian Junior Football League and Quebec Junior Football League are for players aged 18–22. Post-secondary institutions compete in U Sports football for the Vanier Cup, and seniors in the Alberta Football League. The Canadian Football Hall of Fame is in Hamilton, Ontario.

The first documented football match was a practice game played on November 9, 1861, at University College, University of Toronto (approximately 400 yards or 370 metres west of Queen's Park). One of the participants in the game involving University of Toronto students was Sir William Mulock, later chancellor of the school. A football club was formed at the university soon afterward, although its rules of play at this stage are unclear.

The first written account of a game played was on October 15, 1862, on the Montreal Cricket Grounds. It was between the First Battalion Grenadier Guards and the Second Battalion Scots Fusilier Guards resulting in a win by the Grenadier Guards 3 goals, 2 rouges to nothing. In 1864, at Trinity College, Toronto, F. Barlow Cumberland, Frederick A. Bethune, and Christopher Gwynn, devised rules based on rugby football. The game gradually gained a following, with the Hamilton Football Club (later the Hamilton Tiger-Cats) formed on November 3, 1869. Montreal Football Club was formed on April 8, 1872. Toronto Argonaut Football Club was formed on October 4, 1873, and the Ottawa Football Club (later the Ottawa Rough Riders) on September 20, 1876. Of those clubs, only the Toronto club is still in continuous operation today.

This rugby-football soon became popular at Montreal's McGill University. McGill challenged Harvard University to a two-game series in 1874, using a hybrid game of English rugby devised by the University of McGill.

The first attempt to establish a proper governing body and to adopt the current set of Rugby rules was the Foot Ball Association of Canada, organized on March 24, 1873, followed by the Canadian Rugby Football Union (CRFU) founded June 12, 1880, which included teams from Ontario and Quebec. Later both the Ontario Rugby Football Union and Quebec Rugby Football Union (ORFU and QRFU respectively) were formed (January 1883), and then the Interprovincial (1907) and Western Interprovincial Football Union (1936) (IRFU and WIFU). The CRFU reorganized into an umbrella organization forming the Canadian Rugby Union (CRU) in 1891. The immediate forerunner to the current Canadian Football League was established in 1956 when the IRFU and WIFU formed an umbrella organization, the Canadian Football Council (CFC). In 1958, the CFC left the CRU to become the "Canadian Football League" (CFL).

The Burnside rules closely resembling American football (which are similar rules developed by Walter Camp for that sport) that were incorporated in 1903 by the ORFU, were an effort to distinguish it from a more rugby-oriented game. The Burnside Rules had teams reduced to 12 men per side, introduced the snap-back system, required the offensive team to gain 10 yards on three downs, eliminated the throw-in from the sidelines, allowed only six men on the line, stated that all goals by kicking were to be worth two points and the opposition was to line up 10 yards from the defenders on all kicks. The rules were an attempt to standardize the rules throughout the country. The CIRFU, QRFU, and CRU refused to adopt the new rules at first. Forward passes were not allowed in the Canadian game until 1929, and touchdowns, which had been five points, were increased to six points in 1956, in both cases several decades after the Americans had adopted the same changes. The primary differences between the Canadian and American games stem from rule changes that the American side of the border adopted but the Canadian side did not (originally, both sides had three downs, goal posts on the goal lines, and unlimited forward motion, but the American side modified these rules and the Canadians did not). The Canadian field width was one rule that was not based on American rules, as the Canadian game was played in wider fields and stadiums than its American counterpart.

The Grey Cup was established in 1909, after being donated by Albert Grey, 4th Earl Grey, Governor General of Canada, as the championship of teams under the CRU for the Rugby Football Championship of Canada. Initially an amateur competition, it eventually became dominated by professional teams in the 1940s and early 1950s. The ORFU, the last amateur organization to compete for the trophy, withdrew from competition after the 1954 season. The move ushered in the modern era of Canadian professional football, culminating in the formation of the present-day Canadian Football League in 1958.

articles.title: Reclaiming Indigenous culinary histories in Nepal
paragraphs: Food enriches our soul. It makes us who we are. However, the emergence of cosmopolitanism and global and local food politics has sidelined Indigenous food, not to mention the traditions and rituals associated with them.

“Over the last decades, ever since the country was opened up to the outside world in the 1950s, in search of a national food identity, the staple daal bhaat, a nutrient-dense combination of lentils and rice accompanied by vegetables, has been elevated to Nepal’s national dish,” writes Binti Gurung, a food historian and founder of Natural Roots Foundation, an organization dedicated to documenting, preserving, and promoting Indigenous Himalayan food heritage, traditional recipes, and local knowledge in Nepal. “The national food narrative that is being set completely obscures the varied regional histories and food practices of the Indigenous peoples.”
The Foundation, established in 2017, promotes the many varieties of food that have become neglected in Nepal, especially the plants and herbs that can be foraged in the forests and mountains.

Working with Aama Samuha, a collective of women’s groups set up to maintain cultural traditions and support communal activities in Nepali villages, she has been documenting and archiving the food knowledge primarily held by Indigenous women in Nepal.

The Lekhali Cookbook, authored by Gurung, draws its name from lekh, the high ridges in Nepal, and highlights the rich food tradition shared by women’s groups from Nepal’s Mustang, Manang, Lamjung, and Gorkha districts.
Sanjib Chaudhary of Global Voices caught up with Binti Gurung to talk about her work on food heritage. The interview has been edited for length and clarity.
Sanjib Chaudhary (SC): Can you introduce yourself and tell us a bit about your work?

Binti Gurung (BG): Before talking about the food heritage of Nepal, it’s necessary to mention that knowing the broader political and historical context of the country is important because a lot of what my work looks into connects with understanding of the past.

The pivotal moment can be attributed to the 1950s, when the absolutist regime came to an end . As a country, Nepal had remained closed off to the outside world for so long that very little was understood about Nepali society, particularly its food practices.

Within this environment of reaching out to the past events that happened in this land, uncovering the stories of the people, and mainly breaking down and deconstructing the idea of “Nepali-ness,” lies the understanding of our food heritage.

I myself come from what used to be called a Gurung country until the 1970s. I know something about our collective history as Gurung people, and that my great-grandfather on the maternal side was a mukhiya, a tribal chief somewhere in that Gurung country. There are no written documents about our lineage, apart from the knowledge that remains in the tongue. I take pride in that, but it also means some knowledge has not been transmitted.

My paternal grandfather was the first person to be educated because of his connection to British India, after which he did a lot in his village, which included donating some of his personal land to the village school. Whereas I am the first in my family to go to university, learn English (like the rest of my generation), and read history.
SC: Food sovereignty is a burning issue for Indigenous peoples. Can you give us an overview of what challenges Indigenous communities in Nepal are facing with regard to food sovereignty?

BG: Even though the constitution of 2015 has given recognition to the right to food, how does it translate to the many Indigenous groups accessing their food? Are the Indigenous peoples who have been living by the rivers and the forests able to access the foods that they have learned to process, collect, and eat?

For the communities that still live in or near the forest, how are their relationships affected when forests are turned into national parks? Do the Indigenous peoples who have been relying on these ancestral food practices have access? Can the state recognize and permit it?
When we start to think this way, we go beyond the conversation about food sovereignty because then we have to talk about the land and the peoples who inhabit it, and their connection to it.

SC: Nepal is a multi-ethnic country, and communities have their own food and agriculture systems. However, food politics is prevalent, with some communities claiming a particular dish as solely theirs. What’s your take on this?

BG: I think it is impossible to claim any particular dish as solely belonging to only one community. After all, we live in a shared world. We are beings in constant interaction with the land. Like any living practice that is evolving, our food practices are also in motion; it is not a static, fixed thing.

What may be helpful is to think about how a dish or food practice evolved. Or even to try to understand how it has evolved the way it has, including the factors of influence. Even though we think of Nepali communities having their own food systems, if we look underneath somewhere, we can find some similar practices.

One example is the way food is harvested from the forest; this particular practice, whether in the high mountains, hills, or the Terai, remains similar. Of course, how this practice is treated by those not practicing is an entirely different thing.

SC: It’s high time we promote Indigenous food in a global space. Can you tell us about your recent book “The Lekhali Cookbook: Indigenous Food Heritage from the Highlands of Nepal” and the dishes you’d like to share with a wider audience?

BG: This book has been in the making for a very long time. When I started doing this work in 2017, at some point it felt very urgent to understand the issues around it, and gradually it became important to start documenting in a written way because a lot had been unknown.

There may be many factors why the conversation around food heritage has remained so obscure, but one that I attribute strongly to is our own political history that has shaped the Indigenous experiences.

articles.title: A new Democratic Congress will view Trump’s harsh Cuba policy skeptically – but that doesn’t mean a change is coming soon
paragraphs: The so-called “ blue tsunami ” that hit the United States in the midterm elections is causing ripples around the world.
Having won a historic victory, congressional Democrats now appear poised to challenge the Trump administration’s conduct of foreign affairs .
The Iran war, support for Ukraine and the management of Venezuelan oil certainly all appear to be on the agenda of some Democrats.
The flipping of the House and Senate from Republican to Democratic control has also led to speculation that members of Congress may also wish to challenge Trump’s Cuba policy .

After all, the United States’ position on Cuba has swung in recent decades, depending on the balance of power in Washington. An easing of tensions and normalization of relations between the U.S. and Cuba took place under the presidency of Barack Obama, only to be reversed following the election of Donald Trump in 2016. President Joe Biden largely followed Trump’s lead, while making more allowance for activities supporting the Cuban people.

In his second term, however, Trump has pursued an even harder line than before. Since January 2026, the administration has instituted a devastating economic and fuel blockade, prohibiting Cubans from importing oil . This pressure tactic is meant to get the Cuban government to agree to increased economic privatization and political democratization .
While the Cuban government has met certain demands, notably with respect to the economy, it has resolutely refused to change either its personnel or its authoritarian character.
The result of this blockade has been a stalemate and increased hardship for Cubans. As a historian of U.S.-Cuban relations, I saw that hardship firsthand during a visit to Havana in June 2026 .

While I understand the notion that emboldened Democrats may try to force a change in direction of the Trump administration’s foreign policy, including on Cuba, I doubt they will be able to do so. In fact, there are reasons to believe that the midterm results may actually reinforce Republicans’ hard-line approach to the Caribbean island.
Since 1961, at the height of the Cold War, the U.S. government has enforced a rigorous sanctions regime against communist Cuba – the longest-running embargo in modern history.

In January 2026, the Trump administration made that embargo even more severe with the oil importation ban, part of a regional pressure campaign that also saw U.S. forces abduct and remove from office Venezuela’s President Nicolás Maduro, a longtime ally of the Cuban government.
For Cubans, no oil means no electricity . Blackouts, already a problem, have become longer and more frequent.

Absent electricity, Cubans have no regular access to running water . Disease, from mosquitoes, other pests and unsafe water, has increased dramatically . Cuba’s once much-praised medical system often cannot treat patients unless they bring their own drugs and supplies.
Inflation has soared and tourists have stopped coming, while industrial and agricultural production has declined dramatically.

Cubans hate the U.S. embargo for contributing to this misery. At the same time, many also blame their government. During my last visit, Cubans I spoke with told me that they believe their leaders are more concerned with protecting their power and privileges than with the welfare of the average Cuban.
For many Cubans, this indifference explains why President Miguel Díaz-Canel and his allies have rejected the Trump administration’s central demand of surrendering their monopoly on power.
Trump’s demands, blockade and the threat of military force have led to some concessions by Cuba’s leaders.
During the past year, Cuba’s government has released some political prisoners and permitted greater foreign investment, most notably from Cuban Americans .
The government in Havana has also expanded the range of legally permitted private enterprise in Cuba.

But when it comes to the question of power, Díaz-Canel and his allies remain implacable. They know that relinquishing power will cut off the supply of profits from state-owned businesses that flows their way and maintains their opulent lifestyles .
They also argue that Trump has no right to determine the rulers of a sovereign nation.
For the moment, it appears that Díaz-Canel hopes international and domestic politics will compel Trump to turn his attention from Cuba.
No doubt, the “blue wave” of the U.S. midterms has encouraged that belief. If so, I believe the hopes of the Cuban government are probably misplaced.
This is in large part because U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a Cuban American who formerly represented Florida in the U.S. Senate, remains determined to topple the Cuban government.

Rubio has long been a foreign policy hawk and fervent proponent of regime change in Cuba. As secretary of state, he has also been a key figure in the Trump administration’s push to expand American power across Latin America and support right-wing movements and governments.
It is also no secret that Rubio wishes to succeed Trump as president. That has not changed since the midterm elections.

In order to become the Republican nominee for president, Rubio will most likely need to win Florida’s primary. And if he is to win the White House, Rubio will surely need Florida’s electoral votes, especially in light of the results of last week’s election in Texas, which saw a U.S. Senate seat and the governorship turn Democrat.

Rubio’s path to the presidency will be easier if he continues to enjoy the support of South Florida’s Cuban American community, which favors regime change by an overwhelming margin and represent a powerful voting bloc in Florida.
In short, I believe ambition and ideology will provide Rubio with the impetus to refuse all compromise with what remains of Cuba’s communist government.
Interestingly, some Republicans seem uneasy with aspects of America’s Cuba policy, particularly the emphasis on investment opportunities as opposed to democratic change.

Nonetheless, Trump has reasons to push harder on Cuba. The midterm results show that his domestic agenda – and the war in Iran – are vote losers. He may see toppling the Cuban government as a guaranteed “win” for him and his administration, both in terms of legacy and in the eyes of voters.
Of course, Democrats in the new Congress could deny the administration funds to maintain the oil blockade or, in an extreme case, invade Cuba.
Democrats could also exercise Congress’ powers of investigation and oversight.
Though these measures enjoy some support among Democrats, it is far from certain that House or Senate leaders would support them.

After all, the Democratic Congress has other priorities that appear of greater concern to the American people, such as the Iran war, not to mention domestic policy issues, such as healthcare and an “ affordability agenda .”

articles.title: The ongoing efforts to get ecocide recognized at the International Criminal Court
paragraphs: This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “ Justice as infrastructure .” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL ) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here .

In September 2024, Vanuatu, Fiji, and Samoa filed an amendment request at the International Criminal Court (ICC) to get “ecocide” recognized as a crime under international law. The ICC currently recognizes four criminal categories: genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes, and the crime of aggression.

Over two years later, the amendment is still formally pending; but that does not mean environmental activists are waiting around — in fact, many are working both in the public eye and behind the scenes to establish legal infrastructure to protect the environment, combat the climate crisis, and punish those responsible for defiling the planet.

According to an independent expert panel convened by the Stop Ecocide Foundation, ecocide is legally defined as “unlawful or wanton acts committed with knowledge that there is a substantial likelihood of severe and either widespread or long-term damage to the environment being caused by those acts.”
For the countries that backed the proposal, the climate crisis is not an abstract threat; it is a real and present danger with active consequences for their people.

In 2021, Simon Kofe, Tuvalu’s Minister for Justice, Communication and Foreign Affairs, gave a presentation at the international COP26 conference on climate change while standing in knee-deep water to demonstrate how rising sea levels threaten low-lying island nations. Tuvaluan officials are also exploring ways to become the first “ digital nation ” as a backup plan in case rising sea levels submerge all livable land in the archipelago. In Fiji alone, six villages have already been relocated because of climate change, with others in progress and dozens more under assessment. As Vanuatu’s Special Envoy for Climate Change and Environment, Ralph Regenvanu, says, climate damage is “devastating our island economy, submerging our territory, and threatening livelihoods.”

Shortly after the amendment was submitted, it was also backed by the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), which is experiencing increasingly deadly flooding as well as air quality issues related to exploitative mining operations .
Tuvulu’s Foreign Minister delivers an address to COP26, while standing in knee-deep water to illustrate how rising sea levels threaten Pacific nations. Image from Simon Kofe’s Facebook . Fair use.

It is not a coincidence that those who are pushing hardest for these legal mechanisms are those most affected by the climate crisis. These nations did little to cause the crisis, while major superpowers like the U.S., China, and Europe, as well as the corporations that bolster them, have made billions by exploiting and polluting the environment unchecked.

Meanwhile, those who suffer from the consequences of our eroding climate have limited legal recourse against the corporations and states most responsible. This juxtaposition is where the argument to make ecocide an international crime comes in.

“We are taking bold and necessary action to address these challenges and encourage other vulnerable states to take note of our newly tabled proposal to bring ecocide to the ICC. Legal recognition of severe and widespread environmental harm holds significant potential to ensure justice and, crucially, to deter further destruction.”

The International Criminal Court was formally established in 2002 to prosecute individuals for grave international crimes (not to be confused with the International Court of Justice, which settles legal disputes between countries).

Environmental crimes are particularly tricky, as traditional legal accountability measures tend to rely on specific individuals or property that have been harmed in order to pursue legal action. In cases where polluters are contributing to a broader destructive pattern, the legal standing becomes murky. This theory has been tested numerous times as individuals have sought to sue fossil fuel companies in civil court for their destructive practices and malfeasance, with most cases largely unsuccessful.

Supporters say that if the proposed amendment were successful, it would give ICC prosecutors the power to hold individuals, such as the executives of large polluting companies or heads of state, responsible in cases like massive oil spills or the deforestation of essential rainforests.

While there have been a series of recent valiant attempts to sue fossil fuel corporations in civil court for covering up evidence that their activities were causing global warming, the defendants have largely been able to get away scot-free. … Criminalizing ecocide would fill this legal gap, and allow individuals (and companies in some jurisdictions) to be prosecuted for engaging in acts with knowledge that they are substantially likely to damage the environment, without the need to show harm to any individual person.

To add a crime to the Rome Statute, a proposal must win a two-thirds majority vote within the court’s Assembly of States Parties. Even then, an amendment to the statute’s crimes provisions would bind only the states that accept it, and the court could not prosecute nationals or territory of states that do not.

The Rome Statute has 123 signatory parties — a number that does not include China, India, or the U.S., the world’s three largest contributors to greenhouse gas emissions. The U.S., in particular, under current President Donald Trump’s administration, has backed away from climate commitments in recent years, including withdrawing from the UN’s 2015 Paris Climate Agreement . It has also become increasingly hostile toward the court itself, as the Trump administration imposed sanctions on individual ICC prosecutors and judges beginning in early 2025. Then, in a September 2026 address to the UN General Assembly, Trump urged all member states to withdraw from the treaty altogether, and, weeks later, in October 2026, he imposed sweeping sanctions on the court itself .

With the biggest emitters outside the court, and Washington working to undermine it, advocates are looking beyond The Hague and ICC reform. As legal watchdogs argue, the end goal is not merely to get the ICC to recognize ecocide — though that would be an excellent first step — rather, if the ICC were to establish a framework for prosecuting international environmental crimes, through an amendment or merely by adapting its existing policies, this could push ratifying states to update their domestic penal codes and adopt policies to protect and preserve their own ecosystems, and also prosecute those who violate them.
Even though the proposal has thus far not been adopted by the ICC, the court has not stood still.

articles.title: Space probe
paragraphs: A space probe is an uncrewed robotic spacecraft designed to explore outer space and transmit scientific data back to Earth. Space probes are used to investigate the Moon, planets, moons, asteroids, comets, the Sun, and interstellar space – it then becomes an interstellar probe. Unlike artificial satellites, which usually remain in orbit around Earth, probes are sent beyond Earth orbit toward other celestial bodies or into deep space.

The first space probes were developed during the early years of the Space Age in the late 1950s. Among the earliest missions were the Soviet Luna probes and the American Pioneer program. Early probes were intended to study the Moon, while later missions expanded to Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and other bodies in the Solar System.

Space probes can be divided into several types according to their mission profile. A flyby probe passes near a celestial body without entering orbit. An orbiter enters orbit around a target body for long-term observation. A lander reaches the surface of a planet or moon, while a rover is capable of moving across the surface. Atmospheric probes descend through an atmosphere to study its composition and weather conditions.

Many space probes have made important scientific discoveries. The Mariner 2 probe became the first spacecraft to successfully fly by another planet when it passed Venus in 1962. The Voyager probes explored the outer planets and later entered interstellar space. The Cassini–Huygens mission studied Saturn and its moons, while the Huygens lander became the first probe to land on Titan in 2005.

Modern space probes continue to explore increasingly distant regions of the Solar System. Voyager 1 became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space in 2012. More recent missions such as Parker Solar Probe and Lucy have been designed to study the Sun and primitive asteroids in unprecedented detail.

articles.title: Nvidia
paragraphs: Nvidia Corporation is an American multinational technology company headquartered in Santa Clara, California. The company develops graphics processing units (GPUs), systems on chips (SoCs), and application programming interfaces (APIs) for gaming, data science, high-performance computing, artificial intelligence (AI) hardware, and mobile and automotive applications. Founded in 1993 by Jensen Huang, Chris Malachowsky, and Curtis Priem, Nvidia is among the largest companies by market capitalization.

Originally focused on GPUs for gaming, Nvidia broadened their usage into other markets, including AI, professional visualization, and supercomputing. The company's product lines include GeForce GPUs for gaming and creative workloads, and professional GPUs for edge computing, scientific research, and industrial applications. In 2025, Nvidia became the first company to surpass US$4 trillion and US$5 trillion in market capitalization, largely driven by the AI boom and soaring demand for its AI data center hardware.

Nvidia was founded on April 5, 1993, by Jensen Huang, a Taiwanese-American electrical engineer who was previously the director of CoreWare at LSI Logic and a microprocessor designer at AMD, Chris Malachowsky, an engineer who worked at Sun Microsystems, and Curtis Priem, who was previously a senior staff engineer and graphics chip designer at IBM and Sun Microsystems. In late 1992, the three men agreed to start the company by sketching out their initial ideas in a meeting at a Denny's roadside diner on Berryessa Road in East San Jose.

At the time, Malachowsky and Priem were frustrated with Sun's management and were looking to leave, but Huang was on "firmer ground", in that he was already running his own division at LSI. The three co-founders discussed a vision of the future for gaming and multimedia markets, which was so compelling that Huang decided to leave LSI and become the chief executive officer of their new startup.

The three co-founders envisioned 3D graphics-based processing as the best trajectory for tackling challenges that had eluded general-purpose computing methods. As Huang later explained: "We also observed that video games were simultaneously one of the most computationally challenging problems and would have incredibly high sales volume. Those two conditions don't happen very often. Video games was our killer app – a flywheel to reach large markets funding huge R&D to solve massive computational problems."

The first problem was who would quit first. Huang's wife, Lori, did not want him to resign from LSI unless Malachowsky resigned from Sun at the same time, and Malachowsky's wife, Melody, felt the same way about Huang. Priem broke that deadlock by resigning first from Sun, effective December 31, 1992. According to Priem, this put pressure on Huang and Malachowsky to not leave him to "flail alone", so they gave notice too. Huang left LSI and "officially joined Priem on February 17", which was also Huang's 30th birthday, while Malachowsky left Sun in early March. In early 1993, the three founders began working together on their new startup in Priem's townhouse in Fremont, California.

With $40,000 in the bank (equivalent to $89,000 in 2025), the company was born. The company subsequently received $20 million of venture capital funding from Sequoia Capital, Sutter Hill Ventures, and others.

During the late 1990s, Nvidia was one of 70 startup companies pursuing the idea that graphics acceleration for video games was the path to the future. Only two survived: Nvidia and ATI Technologies, the latter of which merged into AMD.

Nvidia initially had no name. Priem's first idea was "Primal Graphics", a syllabic abbreviation of two of the founders' last names, but that left out Huang. They soon discovered it was impossible to create a workable name with syllables from all three founders' names, after considering "Huaprimal", "Prihuamal", "Malluapri", etc. The next idea came from Priem's idea for the name of Nvidia's first product. Priem originally wanted to call it the "GXNV", as in the "next version" of the GX graphics chips which he had worked on at Sun. Then Huang told Priem to "drop the GX", resulting in the name "NV". Priem made a list of words with the letters "NV" in them. At one point, Malachowsky and Priem wanted to call the company NVision, but that name was already taken by a manufacturer of toilet paper. Both Priem and Huang have taken credit for coming up with the name Nvidia, from "invidia", the Latin word for "envy". After the company outgrew Priem's townhouse, its original headquarters office was in Sunnyvale, California.

In late 1999, Nvidia released the GeForce 256 (NV10), its first product expressly marketed as a GPU, which was most notable for introducing onboard transformation and lighting (T&L) to consumer-level 3D hardware. Running at 120 MHz and featuring four-pixel pipelines, it implemented advanced video acceleration, motion compensation, and hardware sub-picture alpha blending. The GeForce outperformed existing products by a wide margin.

Because its products were performing well, Nvidia won the contract to develop the graphics hardware for Microsoft's Xbox game console, which included a $200 million advance. However, the project took many of its best engineers away from other projects. In the short term this did not matter, and the GeForce 2 GTS shipped in the summer of 2000. In December 2000, Nvidia reached an agreement to acquire the intellectual assets of its one-time rival 3dfx, a pioneer in consumer 3D graphics technology leading the field from the mid-1990s until 2000. The acquisition process was finalized in April 2002.

In the early-to-mid 2000s, the company invested over a billion dollars to develop CUDA, a software platform and API that enabled GPUs to run massively parallel programs for a broad range of compute-intensive applications. The CUDA platform created a self-reinforcing cycle for Nvidia. As the company expanded wider support for the platform CUDA, it helped Nvidia draw in more developers, leading to further research breakthroughs using Nvidia technology, which attracted more developers and increased the demand for Nvidia hardware. The number of CUDA developers worldwide grew from 1 million in 2018 to 2 million in 2021 and reached 5 million by 2024. By 2025, Nvidia controlled more than 80% of the market for GPUs used in training and deploying AI models, and provided chips for over 75% of the world's TOP500 supercomputers. The company has also expanded into gaming hardware and services, with products such as the Shield Portable, Shield Tablet, and Shield TV, and operates the GeForce Now cloud gaming service. Furthermore, it has developed the Tegra line of mobile processors for smartphones, tablets, and automotive infotainment systems.
In 2001, Standard & Poor's selected Nvidia to replace the departing Enron in the S&P 500 stock index, meaning that index funds would need to hold Nvidia shares going forward.

articles.title: A convincing vegan meat alternative needs both taste and texture – here’s how food scientists manufacture them
paragraphs: This Thanksgiving, you may sit down to a table laden with mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce, vegetables and a golden-brown turkey. And, if you have any vegetarians or vegans in your family, you may even see a plant-based meat alternative. But how do food scientists make something taste and look similar to turkey entirely from plants?

Plant-based meat alternatives have become an increasingly prominent part of the food industry, driven partly by concerns about the sustainability of conventional meat production and the search for additional protein sources. One life-cycle assessment found that plant-based patties had a 77% lower climate impact than the Brazilian beef patties examined, although the results varied depending on the production systems and environmental measures considered.

But making a convincing meat alternative is not as simple as replacing animal protein with plant protein. How do you turn ingredients from peas, soybeans or wheat into something that looks, tastes and feels like meat?

When people think about protein, foods such as chicken, beef, eggs and milk often come to mind. However, plants are also important sources of protein . Soybeans, peas, wheat, lentils and other legumes contain proteins that can be extracted and used in food products.

Soy and pea proteins are widely used in plant-based meat alternatives . Wheat protein, or gluten, can also contribute to their structure and chewy texture. Researchers are also exploring other sources, including fava beans and mung beans, to expand the range of ingredients available.

But plant proteins behave differently. Some absorb more water, while others bind fat or form structures that hold ingredients together. These properties influence how a food feels when you bite into it. Choosing a protein therefore involves understanding how it behaves during processing, not just its nutritional value.
Why is making meat from plants so difficult?

Think about biting into a piece of roasted turkey breast. Its texture comes from the arrangement of muscle fibers, along with connective tissue, water and fat. Together, these components create firmness, juiciness and the chewing experience you associate with meat.

Plant proteins have structures that are different from animal muscle proteins. Mixing pea or soy protein with water does not automatically create meatlike fibers. Food scientists use processing methods that organize these proteins into structures that more closely resemble muscle.

Flavor matters, too. Fat adds juiciness and carries flavor compounds, while heating creates familiar roasted and savory aromas. A convincing meat alternative must bring together the right ingredients and processing conditions to reproduce these qualities.

One widely used method is extrusion . Protein-rich ingredients are mixed with water and pushed through a machine that applies heat and pressure while mixing the material. These forces unfold the proteins and help them interact.

As the mixture cools, the proteins form aligned, fibrous structures that resemble some features of meat. High-moisture extrusion uses more water during processing, which produces fibrous products with a more meatlike texture.

The final structure depends on factors such as the protein source, moisture content, temperature and processing conditions. These factors influence how proteins interact and form the fibrous structures found in plant-based meat alternatives .

Manufacturers can also add fats, starches, flavorings and other ingredients to improve the eating experience. Small changes in formulation or processing can make a considerable difference, affecting whether a product is firmer, softer, chewier or better at retaining moisture.
Another emerging approach is 3D food printing. Like a conventional 3D printer, a food printer builds an object layer by layer, depositing edible materials according to a digital design.

Our research explores protein-based food inks: mixtures designed to flow through a printer nozzle and hold their shape once deposited. Developing the right formulation is challenging because the material must be fluid enough to print but still firm enough to retain its shape. Researchers are applying similar principles to explore printing plant-based meat alternatives.

Instead of relying only on conventional manufacturing methods, 3D printing could allow researchers to control how different ingredients are arranged. For example, you could potentially deposit protein-rich materials and fat-containing ingredients in specific patterns to create different structures and textures.

Recent research on the 3D-printing of plant-protein-based meat analogs highlights how the formulation of the food ink and printing conditions influence how accurately a product can be printed and whether it holds its shape. However, a printed product that looks like meat must still deliver the expected texture, flavor and eating experience.

Plant-based meat alternatives are not necessarily intended to replace traditional meat. They offer consumers additional choices, but making them appealing, affordable and consistent remains a challenge. Scientists continue to study how proteins, ingredients and processing work together to create the textures and flavors people enjoy.

The next time you see a plant-based burger or turkey alternative, remember that making it involves much more than replacing animal protein with plant protein. Technologies such as extrusion and 3D food printing are helping scientists explore new ways to turn plant ingredients into meatlike foods.

articles.title: How does a compass work?
paragraphs: If you’re like me, when you pick up a compass you can’t help but spin it this way and that, to see if you can trick it. It’s hard to resist experimenting with a spooky force we can’t see or feel ourselves. Yet it always turns the compass needle back towards north.

Even in today’s high-tech world, compasses are useful navigation tools. A compass works without power, unlike GPS, and in any weather and lighting conditions, as opposed to navigation using the Sun, stars or landmarks. If you know which way north is, you can determine any direction.
Like all cool phenomena, the explanation of how a compass works is not magic – it’s physics. And people have been making use of this particular aspect of physics for more than 2,000 years .
The earliest versions of the compass were developed in ancient China. They were spoon-shaped and made of lodestones, pieces of the naturally magnetic mineral magnetite.

When allowed to rotate freely, the spoon handle would align itself with a particular direction (north–south). This was used to organise and harmonise environments, as part of a practice you might know as feng shui .

At the time, it was known that some materials were naturally magnetic – able to attract one another. However, it wasn’t clear exactly what was causing a compass to align itself north–south until 1600, when English physicist William Gilbert deduced that Earth itself acted as a giant magnet .
Like all magnets, Earth generates a magnetic field – an invisible region within which its magnetic forces act.

Electricity and magnetism are closely connected. Together, they form one of the fundamental interactions in physics: electromagnetism . Magnetic fields can be created by electric currents, which are the movements of charged particles; a changing magnetic field can also induce an electrical current.
Our planet spins around an axis once roughly every 24 hours, which is why we have a night and day cycle . The end points of this axis are the North Pole and the South Pole.

Beneath Earth’s surface, in the outer core, electrically conducting liquid metals circulate in convective currents . This movement generates electrical currents. Paired with Earth’s rotation around its axis, these currents maintain a global-scale magnetic field . It extends out into space like a giant, invisible bubble, known as the magnetosphere.
And it’s this global-scale magnetic field that allows a compass to work.

In modern compasses, a magnetised metal needle has replaced the lodestone spoon. That needle is mounted on a low-friction pivot so it has minimal resistance to the effects of external magnetic fields.
As a result, unless there’s a magnet directly nearby, the needle will align itself with Earth’s magnetic north–south direction.

If you’ve ever found that a compass needle didn’t perfectly align with north–south, it might be because it detected a localised magnetic field. Electrical devices such as your phone produce weak magnetic fields. These can affect a compass, causing it to deviate from Earth’s magnetic field.

All magnets have two opposite points – a “north” pole and a “south” pole. If you have two magnets, opposite poles (north–south) will pull towards each other, while the same poles (south–south or north–north) will push away.
The next bit will seem a little confusing, but it’s key to understand why compasses point towards the geographic north.

Because opposites attract, the “north” arrow on a compass points towards the “south” pole of Earth’s global-scale magnetic field – the area where field lines point down into Earth’s surface. Despite it having a magnetic polarity of “south”, we call this spot the north magnetic pole because it’s located close to the geographic North Pole in the Arctic.
Earth also has a magnetic south pole, and you guessed it – it’s located near the South Pole in Antarctica, while being the “north” counterpart of Earth’s magnetic field.

The magnetic poles don’t align perfectly with the poles of Earth’s rotational axis. The reason for this is that Earth’s magnetic field is dynamic. The ever-changing motion of liquid metal in Earth’s outer core means the global magnetic field changes, too.
In fact, the magnetic north and south poles slowly change their locations, and the entire magnetic field has even flipped its polarity in the past, making the two switch places.

Earth’s magnetic field also acts as a protective barrier from space weather generated by our Sun: there’s a constant stream of charged particles coming our way, known as solar wind. The global magnetic field helps to shield Earth and our atmosphere.

Mars, by contrast, no longer has a strong global-scale magnetic field to act as a protective shield. Interactions with solar wind have, over time, contributed to the loss of much of Mars’ atmosphere .
So, the same invisible magnetic field that turns a compass needle also plays a much bigger role in helping to keep Earth our home .

articles.title: NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached 1 light-day from Earth, the first human-made object in space to reach that distance
paragraphs: In the summer of 2027, the Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 spacecraft will each reach a milestone in time. On Sept. 5 and Aug. 20, respectively, they will each have spent 50 years in space .

During their journeys, they first explored the planets of the outer solar system, then traveled to the edge of the solar system. Eventually, they passed into the interstellar medium : the space between stars. Although not the first spacecraft ever launched, these are now the two oldest spacecraft still operating.

But before the spacecraft hit their semicentennial, Voyager 1 will also reach a milestone in distance. On Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16 a.m. EST, Voyager 1 will become the first human-built object of any kind to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth . At that point, it will have traveled about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers), more than four times the distance from the Sun to Pluto. Afterward, it will take light, including communication signals, 24 hours to travel between the spacecraft and Earth.
This achievement is remarkable on many levels. This spacecraft, a functioning relic of 1970s technology, has survived well past its expected lifespan.

Of course, the spacecraft no longer works as well as it did in its prime. Eight of its original 10 instruments are not operating, and the output from its plutonium-238 power source degrades a little bit each year. Every so often, a lost signal or technical failure puts Voyager 1 in the headlines again. And, within the next decade, scientists may receive the last signal ever from this far-flung object.

But, at least for now, both Voyagers continue to send back data that is helping scientists characterize the unknown territory beyond the solar system. As a space history curator responsible for the National Air and Space Museum’s planetary science collection, I’ve studied how space exploration has changed dramatically over the past 50 years.

Through it all, the Voyager probes have consistently collected valuable scientific data that has shaped researchers’ understanding of the solar system – and even what lies beyond it. They’ve also helped set public expectations for what a successful mission looks like.
Voyager 1 launched on Sept. 5, 1977, 16 days after the identical Voyager 2, from NASA’s launch complex in Cape Canaveral, Florida. Voyager 2 launched first, but Voyager 1 quickly overtook it.

These spacecraft were big both in size and in ambition. Each is about the size of a small car, with an extended magnetometer boom, carrying instruments that measure magnetic fields, more than 50 feet (15 meters) long.

Each probe explored the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn and returned images from these planets that had higher resolutions than anything returned by their predecessors, Pioneer 10 and 11 . They imaged the turbulent atmosphere of Jupiter, discovered faint rings around the planet and captured new details of the rings of Saturn and its many moons.

Voyager 2 would go on to explore Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989, completing a grand tour of the solar system, that omitted Pluto. Voyager 1 launched after Voyager 2 so it could be set on a course that took it to Saturn’s largest moon, Titan .

On Nov. 12, 1980, Voyager 1 flew within 4,034 miles (6,492 km) of Titan and returned images of the moon that showed a world shrouded in a dense and substantial atmosphere . Now, several decades later, NASA’s Dragonfly mission is slated to take flight in the mid-2030s and investigate Titan’s atmosphere.

This trajectory allowed the probe to image several of Saturn’s other moons and even discover a few new ones. But it also sent Voyager 1 on a course that flung it away from the plane of the planets’ orbits.

It has been traveling in that direction ever since, crossing several milestones along the way. It crossed the orbit of Pluto in 1989. On Feb. 14, 1990, before powering off its cameras for the last time, it captured a series of 64 images that together became the first “family portrait” of the solar system .

There is no clear definition of what it means to leave the solar system. But Voyager 1 has felt less and less of the Sun’s influence as it moves into interstellar space. In December 2004, it crossed the “ termination shock ”: the outer boundary of the influence of the high-energy particles that make up the solar wind .

On Aug. 15, 2012, it left the protection of the Sun’s magnetic field, making it more susceptible to cosmic radiation . As it crossed this boundary, its instruments detected a sparse layer of superheated plasma : charged gas atoms that are so energetic that their electrons are ripped away from their nuclei . Scientists nicknamed this boundary the “ Wall of Fire .”
The spacecraft continues to travel through interstellar space, recording how the space environment changes as you move farther away from the Sun with data from two of its original instruments.

Meanwhile, failing memory, computer glitches, power issues and challenges with an aging propulsion system have led to several nail-biting moments over the past decade in which it seemed scientists might lose contact with the mission forever.
Remarkably, NASA engineers have always found a way to use backup thrusters and reroute data to keep the spacecraft operating, long enough to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.

When talking about the distance from the Earth to the Moon, or from the Earth to Mars or Venus, you’d still use miles or kilometers. But once you travel farther than the distance between Earth and its nearest neighbors, the number of miles starts to increase exponentially.

Outside of the inner solar system, scientists start to use a larger unit of measure: the astronomical unit (AU), one of which equals the distance between the Sun and Earth. The Kuiper Belt, for example, where Pluto is found, covers a wide swath between 30 and 50 AUs from the Sun.

The inner solar system, with Earth and all of the rocky planets, is only an incredibly small fraction of the solar system, and the units of measurement used on Earth don’t really scale well as you move farther away from the planet.

Outside of the solar system, scientists start to talk in terms of time: light-years, or, more precisely, the distance light travels in a year. One light-year is equivalent to 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion km), or 63,241.1 AU. The nearest neighboring star to our solar system is Proxima Centauri, which is about 4.25 light-years away.

articles.title: Sierra Snow Season Spins Up
paragraphs: California’s Sierra Nevada got an early taste of wintry weather when one of the first major snowfalls of the water year arrived on November 13, 2026. A moisture-laden storm delivered heavy rains to lower elevations in the Sacramento area and snow accumulations of around a foot to some mountainous areas. The recent bout of wet weather was the first in a quick succession of Pacific storms bringing rain, snow, and wind to the U.S. West in mid-November.

The MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer) on NASA’s Terra satellite captured this image (right) of fresh snow in the Sierra Nevada on the morning of November 14, during a lull between weather systems. Two days earlier (left), the mountains were mostly bare, with snow appearing only at the highest elevations.

Nearly 12 inches (30 centimeters) of snow fell at Donner Pass, northwest of Lake Tahoe, on November 13, according to the Central Sierra Snow Laboratory . The accumulation snarled traffic on Interstate 80 in the area, prompting officials to close the highway in both directions that evening. To the south, the ski resort at Mammoth Mountain reported 9 to 13 inches (23 to 33 centimeters) of new snow, and officials at Yosemite National Park closed several roads ahead of the storm.

More wet weather and mountain snow are forecast to follow . The National Weather Service (NWS) issued a winter storm warning for portions of the Sierras above 5,000 feet (1,500 meters) in elevation from November 18 to 20. NWS warned of difficult-to-impossible travel conditions, gusty winds, and snow accumulations of around 4 feet (120 centimeters) possible above 8,000 feet (2,400 meters).

articles.title: US and Iran once practiced diplomacy through archaeology – that legacy need not lie in ruins
paragraphs: When a U.S. airstrike struck Tehran’s Arg Square on March 2, 2026, Golestan Palace was not the target. But it was close enough.

The missile’s impact blew out windows across the palace complex and damaged some of its elaborate 19th-century interiors. In photographs taken afterward, pieces of its celebrated mirrorwork lay scattered across the floor.

Golestan is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the great surviving monuments of Iran’s Qajar dynasty, which ruled from 1789 until 1925. Within hours of the strike, UNESCO reported the damage and noted that cultural property is protected under international law during armed conflict.

The palace was not only an early casualty of the U.S.-Iran war, but a symbolically potent one, too. And as my colleague Mehrnoush Soroush at the Center for Ancient Middle Eastern Landscapes has documented, Golestan is not alone. Since the war in Iran began in February 2026, reports of damage to heritage sites have poured in from all across Iran.

I know that damaged buildings — no matter how valuable — cannot compare with the human costs of war. But the images from Golestan have particular resonance to me, an archaeologist who studies the history of relations between Iran and the United States . It also cuts against a history of cooperation between American and Iranian archaeologists, in which Americans worked to preserve, rather than destroy, Iranian heritage.
I have spent years researching how archaeologists, museums and cultural officials from the two countries worked together before the Iranian Revolution of 1979 .

My earlier research has examined how archaeology became entangled with American foreign aid and Iranian development programs during the 1960s, and I am currently writing a book on the history of U.S.-Iranian heritage diplomacy over the past century.

I believe that history offers another way of thinking about what has been lost in the current conflict. Long before Iran and the U.S. became adversaries, cultural heritage provided a setting in which people from the two countries learned how to work together.

American archaeologists began excavating in Iran in the early 1930s . In those days, the relationship was unequal: American museums sought access to archaeological sites and, under agreements with the Iranian government, received portions of the objects they excavated under the colonial system of partage . As a result, museums across the U.S. still hold substantial collections of Iranian antiquities.

The terms of the relationship changed considerably during the 1960s, as the U.S. and Iran intensified their connections. At the same time that thousands of American professionals, educators, businesspeople, scholars and others came to work and live in Iran, the country revised its antiquities laws and expanded its own archaeological institutions, universities and museums, resulting in, among other things, a major tourism boom .

American archaeologists still wanted permission to dig at Iranian sites, but they increasingly operated within a system controlled by Iranian officials. In return, American institutions contributed funding and access to laboratories, specialist knowledge, graduate education and connections to an international scholarly community.

American archaeological projects in Iran drew on large networks of such connections. Scholars working on the Deh Luran Plain in southwestern Iran, for example, depended on Iranian government agencies, the U.S. Embassy, American universities and museums, development organizations and scientific laboratories. Botanical remains, animal bones and other materials moved through specialist laboratories abroad, while Iranian officials worked alongside foreign researchers in the field.

By the 1970s, fieldwork projects were increasingly becoming joint enterprises, based on formal partnerships between institutions and cooperative leadership. Iranian archaeological authorities employed American specialists to help survey areas threatened by dams and other development projects, while Iranian archaeologists increasingly took leading roles in the field. Meanwhile, students moved in greater numbers between Tehran, Chicago, Philadelphia and New York. Museums organized traveling exhibitions, and Iran hosted international scholarly congresses devoted to its history and archaeology.
It can’t be ignored that these collaborations flourished during a period when Iran, under Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi, was a close American ally .

While the terms of the relationship increasingly favored Iran, they were still marked by geopolitical inequalities. American universities and museums possessed resources that Iranian institutions often lacked – not only financially and in terms of human capital, but physically, in the form of collections of artifacts that had previously been taken out of Iran.
Yet the collaborations also developed lives of their own, as American scholars returned year after year.

The Islamic Revolution exposed both how extensive and fragile this network was. Even as the crisis that began in 1978 deepened, American archaeologists did not initially assume that their Iranian partnerships were finished. At Malyan, the remains of ancient Anshan, archaeologist William Sumner proposed continuing to pay a watchman to protect the site, while maintaining contact with Iranian colleagues so research could eventually resume.

That did not come to pass. And much of the American-Iranian archaeological enterprise collapsed as diplomatic relations between the two countries soured after the Islamic Republic took 52 American diplomats and civilians hostage in 1979 and Washington sided with Baghdad during the Iran-Iraq War in the 1980s.
But the example of the 1960s and ‘70s points toward a sometimes less visible part of diplomacy: relationships accumulated through repeated practical work.

International relations expert Trita Parsi makes this point in his history of the negotiations that produced the 2015 Iran nuclear agreement . In “ Losing an Enemy,” based on interviews with participants on both sides, Parsi describes the working relationship that developed between U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif.

This is not to say that their personal rapport produced the nuclear agreement by itself. Naturally, presidents had to authorize negotiations, diplomats at all levels had to find compromises, and both governments had to conclude that an agreement served their interests. But contemporary reporting described that relationship as one built on professional respect and repeated close proximity. In other words, Kerry and Zarif spent enough time negotiating together to understand each other’s constraints and establish a working relationship despite the hostility between their two governments.

That kind of personal working relationship can assist diplomacy – not just at the highest levels but more broadly across civil society. Sports diplomacy has long been acknowledged; so too the sharing of zoological “gifts.” My research shows that archaeology has long had an important a place in these kinds of cultural exchanges as well.
Today, Iranian conservation specialists are sorting and cataloging shattered fragments from Golestan Palace while attempting to repair damage at heritage sites around the country .

articles.title: 1980 Irpinia earthquake
paragraphs: The 1980 Irpinia earthquake (Italian: Terremoto dell'Irpinia) took place in Italy on 23 November 1980, with a moment magnitude of 6.9 and a maximum Mercalli intensity of X (Extreme). It left at least 2,483 people dead, at least 7,700 injured, and 250,000 homeless.

The earthquake struck at 18:34 UTC (19:34 local) on 23 November 1980, centered on the village of Castelnuovo di Conza, Campania, Southern Italy. The first jolt was followed by 90 aftershocks. There were three main shocks, each with epicenters in a different place, within 80 seconds. The largest shock registered a peak acceleration of 0.38 g, with 10 seconds of motion greater than 0.1 g. The three main shocks combined produced 70 seconds of shaking greater than 0.01 g. Thus the shaking was severe and lasted a long time.

The focal mechanism corresponded to normal and significant left-lateral strike-slip movement. The rupture dimensions was estimated to be 14 km × 40 km (8.7 mi × 24.9 mi) based on the aftershock distribution. The study of near-field strong motion and leveling records revealed a complex rupture process comprising three subevents. Overall, the rupture on complex fault systems propagated bilaterally along a mostly northwest–southeast trend.

Towns in the province of Avellino were hit the hardest. In Sant'Angelo dei Lombardi, 300 were killed, including 27 children in an orphanage, and 80 percent of the town was destroyed and many historical buildings were left in ruins as the town never fully recovered as of 2021. One hundred were killed in Balvano when a medieval church collapsed during Sunday services. The towns of Lioni, Conza della Campania (near the epicenter), and Teora were destroyed, and dozens of structures in Naples were levelled, including a 10-story apartment building. Damage was spread over more than 26,000 km2 (10,000 sq mi), including Naples and Salerno.

The Italian government spent 59 trillion lire (equivalent to €151 billion in 2020) on reconstruction, while other nations sent contributions. West Germany contributed 32 million United States dollars (USD) and the United States US$70 million.

However, in the early 1990s a major corruption scandal emerged. Of the billions of lire that were earmarked for aid to the victims and rebuilding, the largest part disappeared from the earthquake reconstruction funds in the 1980s. Of the $40 billion spent on earthquake reconstruction, an estimated $20 billion went to create an entirely new social class of millionaires in the region, $6.4 billion went to the criminal Camorra, whereas another $4 billion went to politicians in bribes. Only the remaining $9.6 billion, a quarter of the total amount, was actually spent on people's needs.
The Camorra entered the construction industry after the quake.

articles.title: Rose Revolution
paragraphs: The Rose Revolution or Revolution of Roses (Georgian: ვარდების რევოლუცია, romanized: vardebis revolutsia) was a nonviolent change of power that occurred in Georgia in November 2003. The event was brought about by widespread protests over the disputed parliamentary elections and culminated in the resignation of President Eduard Shevardnadze, which marked the end of Soviet-era leadership in the country. The revolution derives its name from the climactic moment, when demonstrators led by Mikheil Saakashvili stormed the Parliament session with red roses in hand.

The revolution was led by Shevardnadze's former political allies, Mikheil Saakashvili, Nino Burjanadze and Zurab Zhvania. Consisting of twenty days of protests from 3 to 23 November 2003, the Revolution triggered new presidential and parliamentary elections in Georgia, which brought the National Movement–Democrats coalition to the power. The death of Zurab Zhvania in uncertain circumstances and the withdrawal of Nino Burjanadze into opposition eventually established the United National Movement as the single ruling party.

According to the United States Department of State, with the sweeping reforms brought by the Rose Revolution, Georgia moved "from a near-failed state in 2003 to a relatively well-functioning market economy in 2014". The Rose Revolution is considered one of the early examples of colour revolutions. It was marked by strong role of non-governmental organizations and student activism.

The Citizens' Union of Georgia (CUG) had been the ruling party for most of Eduard Shevardnadze's Presidency, and represented the interests of Shevardnadze loyalists. The ineffectiveness of the government and the decreasing popularity of the regime led to the defection of numerous parliamentary deputies from the ruling party in 2000. The first group to leave the CUG represented the business community and would go on to form the New Rights Party (NRP) in 2001. This began the collapse of the party, as numerous party officials and deputies defected to join or form other parties. Eduard Shevardnadze himself resigned from the chairmanship of the CUG in September 2001. Fatefully, Mikheil Saakashvili (the Minister of Justice) left the ruling party in September and would form the National Movement opposition party one month later. The defections continued for the next two years, and left the Citizens' Union of Georgia as a far weaker party with support clustered in a few regions, and a leadership notorious for accumulating wealth illegally through their positions in government. The disintegration of the party highlighted the weakness of the Shevardnadze regime and dispersed the political elite amongst a number of new parties and independent platforms.

The collapse of the Citizens' Union of Georgia and more apparent public discontent with Shevardnadze allowed for the formation of numerous new parties after 2000. The ruling party showed its vulnerability in the 2002 local elections, losing decisively to independents and new parties. The local elections saw independents secure 2754 seats, with the New Rights Party(NRP) being the most successful political party, obtaining 551 parliamentary seats. The Citizens' Union of Georgia won only 70 out of approximately 4,850 local parliamentary seats.

Following the disastrous 2002 local elections, Shevardnadze made a concerted attempt to rebuild a political coalition that could support him. The CUG was rebuilt before the 2003 parliamentary election, which was understood to be a key trial before the 2005 presidential election. However, President Shevardnadze's popularity rating had plummeted to around 5%, undermining any attempt to revive the CUG under his leadership. The new CUG further found itself divided over internal disputes, and lacking effective leadership to replace those that had defected.

Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) played a significant role in the Rose Revolution. By the end of 2000, the number of NGOs estimated to be in Georgia numbered around four thousand. The 1997 Civil Code made the registration of an NGO relatively easy, and they operated in Georgia with few restrictions. Though only a small portion of those likely had influence on the government or were successful in lobbying, several had leverage in parliament. While public participation in these NGOs was relatively low, they were ultimately successful in mobilizing the population to play a more active role in government. Two of the most important were the Georgian Young Lawyers' Association and the Liberty Institute, both of which were active in the promotion of human rights and freedom of information legislation before the Rose Revolution.

Shevardnadze had allowed the development of NGOs before the Rose Revolution, and numerous large and relatively uninhibited NGOs were able to operate in Georgia prior to the 2003 parliamentary elections. Georgia's weak economy allowed these NGOs, who were often partially foreign funded, to pay decent salaries that would not have been available in working for the Georgian state. As early as the summer of 2002, there was great concern amongst the leaders of Georgia's most influential NGOs that Shevardnadze was not prepared to relinquish power voluntarily, and that other ways to remove him from power might be necessary. Some of these leaders hoped to make the 'Serbian scenario' a reality in Georgia, in the sense that they wanted to promote non-violent protests to force the resignation of an authoritarian leader. Before the Rose Revolution, a large network of NGOs with foreign financial support already existed in the country that could later coordinate protest.

Foreign support for the Shevardnadze regime declined from 2000 to 2003, with notable figures outwardly calling for a more democratic transition. These included Richard Miles (the US ambassador to Georgia), and allies of the Bush administration, including a visit from James Baker (the former U.S. Secretary of State) who pressured Shevardnadze to accept parallel vote tabulation and pushed for free election standards.

In the three years before the Rose Revolution, foreign financial support for the regime began to become severely limited. Instead, foreign states and organizations gave financial assistance to NGOs and opposition parties within Georgia, worsening the desperate budget situation of the Shevardnadze government. The United States announced a reduction in aid, coinciding with a decision by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to suspend aid to Georgia. As international support for the regime deteriorated (particularly in the West), public perceptions of Shevardnadze's political weakness increased. A significant source of funding for NGOs and election monitoring organizations came from foreign governments and individuals. The U.S. and European governments gave the OSCE (Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe) the funds to support foreign election observers. The U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID)§ spent $1.5 million to computerize Georgia's voter rolls. The Open Society Institute (OSI), funded by George Soros, supported Mikheil Saakashvili and a network of pro-democratic organizations. Western democracy promoters also circulated public opinion polls and scrutinized election data throughout Georgia.
